description.summary: A persistent low-frequency hum reported by a small minority of residents around Taos, New Mexico from the early 1990s onward, investigated by a 1993 university-led panel without identifying a specific source.
description.full: The Taos Hum is a low-frequency humming, droning, or rumbling sound reported by a small fraction of residents in and around Taos, New Mexico, beginning in the early 1990s. Hearers commonly describe a sound resembling a distant diesel engine that is most noticeable indoors and at night. Surveys in the early 1990s indicated that roughly 2% of the local population could hear it, with hearers reporting perceived frequencies in the range of about 32–80 Hz, modulated at approximately 0.5–2 Hz. In 1993, prompted by Taos residents and U.S. Representative Bill Richardson, a multi-institution team led by Joe Mullins (University of New Mexico) and including investigators from Sandia National Laboratories, Los Alamos National Laboratory, and Phillips Laboratory carried out a public investigation of the Hum. The team was unable to identify a single environmental acoustic source. The Taos Hum is one member of a wider class of regional 'Hum' phenomena, including the Bristol Hum (England), the Windsor Hum (Ontario/Michigan), the West Seattle Hum, and the Auckland Hum, which collectively remain unexplained.

etymology.origin: Named for the town of Taos, New Mexico, where the phenomenon was first widely reported and investigated in the early 1990s.
etymology.meaning: 'Hum' in the technical popular sense of a persistent low-frequency drone audible to a minority of nearby observers.
etymology.first_use: Early 1990s in U.S. press coverage of the Taos investigation.

features.description: Hearers report a tonal sensation in the low audible-frequency band; reported frequencies vary between hearers
Hearers describe the sound as pulsing, throbbing, or modulated like a distant engine

features.feature: Most noticeable indoors and at night
features.description: Reports cluster in quiet indoor environments after dark, when ambient noise is lowest

physical.morphology: A persistent acoustic / perceptual phenomenon rather than a discrete 'creature'. Reports describe steady-state, low-amplitude, low-frequency sound with a characteristic rumbling or droning quality.

abilities.description: Hearers commonly report that the Hum interferes with sleep and produces secondary headaches, irritability, and stress
Only ~2% of the surveyed Taos population can hear the Hum, with no consistent demographic predictor beyond a slight skew toward middle-aged adults

patterns: Persistent rather than episodic, often heard daily by sensitive hearers
Most prominent at night in quiet environments

range.description: Reports center on Taos and surrounding Taos County in northern New Mexico, with one early hearer reporting a perceived range of approximately 30 miles (48 km).

hotspots.name: Taos, New Mexico

location.description: Town of Taos and surrounding Taos County

hotspots.notes: Centre of the 1993 University of New Mexico-led investigation.

first_recorded.source: Local Taos press and resident reports cited in U.S. national coverage of the 1993 investigation

peak_activity_periods.description: Initial wave of reports, federal and academic investigation
Continued reports and broader 'Hum' studies online (Glen MacPherson 'World Hum Map', 2012–)

origins.cultural_roots: The Taos Hum belongs to a broader class of late-20th-century 'Hum' reports from quiet residential areas in industrialised countries. Earlier reports of similar sounds (notably the Bristol Hum) had been documented since at least the 1970s.
origins.earliest_accounts: Early 1990s Taos resident reports led to a published petition to the U.S. Congress and a 1993 multi-laboratory investigation.
origins.folklore_connections: Connected to a wider folklore of 'mystery sounds', including the Hessdalen lights for the visual analogue and various Bristol/Windsor/Auckland Hum traditions.

timeline.event: Residents of Taos, New Mexico, begin reporting a persistent low-frequency hum
timeline.significance: Beginning of the documented Taos Hum phenomenon

timeline.event: Multi-institution investigation announced, led by Joe Mullins (University of New Mexico) and supported by Sandia, Los Alamos, and Phillips Laboratory, in response to a petition by Taos residents and U.S. Representative Bill Richardson
timeline.significance: Single largest scientific effort to identify the source of the Taos Hum
timeline.source: Mullins, J. & Kelly, J. (1995), report to U.S. Congress

timeline.event: Mullins and Kelly publish the final 'Taos Hum' investigation report; no specific environmental acoustic source identified
timeline.significance: Establishes the Taos Hum as scientifically unresolved
timeline.source: U.S. Congress / University of New Mexico report

history.modern_era: Reports of the Taos Hum continue, alongside a global community of Hum hearers tracked by Dr. Glen MacPherson's 'World Hum Map and Database' (launched 2012). The Hum remains a topic in low-frequency acoustics, otoacoustic-emissions research, and environmental health literature.

notable.name: 1993 Taos Hum investigation

location.description: Town of Taos and surrounding Taos County, New Mexico

notable.description: In response to a petition from Taos residents and the involvement of U.S. Representative Bill Richardson, an investigation team led by Joe Mullins (University of New Mexico) and supported by Sandia National Laboratories, Los Alamos National Laboratory, and Phillips Laboratory carried out acoustic measurements and a public questionnaire. About 2% of respondents reported hearing the Hum. No single mechanical, electromagnetic, or environmental source was conclusively identified.

credibility.notes: Foundational investigation of the Taos Hum, often cited as the model for later regional Hum studies.

sources: Mullins, J. P. & Kelly, J. (1995) report

audio.name: Mullins/Kelly 1993–1995 acoustic measurements
audio.description: Low-frequency acoustic measurements taken in Taos by the University of New Mexico-led team during the federally supported Hum investigation.
audio.analysis: No clear mechanical or environmental source identified; the team's report concluded that environmental sources alone could not account for the reported hearing experience.

documentary.name: Mullins & Kelly Taos Hum investigation report (1995)
documentary.description: Final report to the U.S. Congress on the Taos Hum investigation by the multi-institution panel.
documentary.analysis: Concluded that the source remained unidentified; recommended further interdisciplinary work.

scientific.name: Spontaneous otoacoustic emissions / individual auditory sensitivity
scientific.description: A widely cited explanation is that some hearers detect their own otoacoustic emissions or are unusually sensitive to ambient low-frequency sounds (e.g. distant infrastructure or geophysical noise) that are below the threshold of most listeners.
evidence_cited: Small fraction of population that hears the Hum
Greater audibility in quiet indoor environments

scientific.name: Industrial / infrastructure low-frequency noise
scientific.description: Other regional Hum phenomena (notably the 2014 Windsor Hum) have been linked to industrial sources; analogous explanations are proposed but unverified for Taos.
evidence_cited: Windsor Hum source attribution to Zug Island industry (Health Canada / University of Windsor study, 2014)

skeptical.name: Tinnitus / psychogenic explanation
skeptical.description: Some commentators argue that the Taos Hum reflects spontaneous tinnitus or psychogenic perception in a sensitive subgroup, given the lack of an identified environmental source and the variation in reported frequency between hearers.
proponents: Various otologists cited in popular reporting
evidence_cited: Variation in reported frequency between individual hearers
Inability of others to detect the sound

stories: Reports compiled by Joe Mullins in the 1993 Taos investigation
Hearer testimonies collected for The X-Files episode 'Drive' (1998), inspired by the Taos Hum
folklore.beliefs: Some Taos hearers attribute the Hum to government or military activity; others to unidentified geophysical or psychic phenomena. Hearers' communities also exist online via the World Hum Map.

literature: Coverage in The New York Times, The Atlantic, and Wired
